specPoints.text: understand how selective breeding can develop animals with desired characteristics

primer.text: Human breeders can steer a bloodline toward the traits people value most. This note follows that steering loop in farm and domestic animals: pick parents that already show the wanted feature, raise their young, keep only the young that express it, and repeat the cycle until the herd or breed reliably carries it, then set that against natural selection.

lessons.title: The Breeding Loop That Shapes Livestock
lessons.opening: Farmers and breeders run a deliberate mating loop. Parents that already show a valued trait — heavy milk yield, meaty carcasses, generous egg size, calm temperament, dense fleece, athletic build — are paired, and from their young only those expressing the trait are kept as the next breeding stock. Every pass of the loop concentrates the trait further, and the loop must run across many generations before the line breeds true.
keyPoints: Breeders choose several unrelated parents that each display the wanted feature, so the next round of matings can avoid brother-to-sister pairings.
Young animals carrying the valued feature are kept and mated on; the rest leave the breeding line.
The selection loop is repeated across many generations before a breed reliably delivers the trait.

Typical livestock goals: dairy cattle, goats and sheep with high milk or meat output; hens laying larger eggs; sheep fleeced for better wool; horses bred for speed and conformation; and pet dogs bred for a mild temperament.
The domestic dog shows how a single ancestor, the wolf, has been moulded into breeds spanning enormous differences in size, build and behaviour.

low.restatement: Pick parents with the trait, mate them, keep the young that show it, and do the same again next generation.
low.analogy: Like a kennel that only ever breeds its fastest dogs — litter after litter, speed climbs as a standard feature.
low.examPointer: The mark scheme rewards the loop, not one mating: parents selected, offspring selected, and the phrase 'repeated over many generations'.

medium.restatement: Several unrelated parents showing the target characteristic are crossed; offspring expressing it are selected as the next breeding stock; iterating the loop over many generations raises how often the desired alleles appear until the breed reliably shows them.
medium.analogy: A football academy that only promotes players who already score heavily — each season's squad starts stronger, and after a decade producing strikers is the academy's norm.
medium.examPointer: Score with contrast pairs: parent selection + offspring selection + generational repetition; dropping any one of the three costs marks.

check.stem: What is the first step in the animal breeding loop for a valued trait?

options.text: Choosing parents that already display the trait
options.explanation: Correct — the loop starts from stock that visibly carries the feature.

options.text: Mating any healthy animals available at random
options.explanation: Random mating gives no direction to the line; the loop depends on deliberate choice.
options.misconception: treats the loop as unselective breeding

options.text: Treating animals with hormones to force the trait
options.explanation: Hormone treatment does not create a heritable breeding goal; the trait must be chosen from parents.

options.text: Waiting for the trait to appear by chance in the herd
options.explanation: Chance appearance is the natural process, not the directed loop breeders run.

check.stem: Why might a breeder pick several different parents rather than a single pair?

options.text: So the next generation can be mated without brother-to-sister pairings
options.explanation: Correct — several chosen parents give unrelated offspring to mate later.

options.text: Because a single pair passes on too many chromosomes
options.explanation: Chromosome count is fixed per species; the reason is about avoiding related matings.

options.text: Because several parents guarantee identical offspring
options.explanation: Sexual reproduction never guarantees identical offspring; the point is variety among chosen stock.

options.text: Because each parent contributes the same mutation
options.explanation: The parents are chosen for visible desired features, not for shared mutations.

check.stem: Which pairing goal belongs to selective breeding of livestock?

options.text: Dairy cows giving higher milk yields
options.explanation: Correct — milk output is a standard livestock selection goal.

options.text: Wild wolves regaining their hunting range
options.explanation: Range recovery is a conservation aim, not a breeding goal on farm stock.

options.text: Cattle surviving without any human care
options.explanation: Farm animals are managed; independence from care is not a selection target.

options.text: Sheep developing camouflage against predators
options.explanation: Camouflage is not among the usual livestock traits; wool, milk, meat and temperament are.

check.stem: The domestic dog descended from wolves is a standard example of selective breeding because…

options.text: breeds from one ancestor differ enormously in size, build and temperament
options.explanation: Correct — one ancestral stock now spans huge human-directed variation.

options.text: every breed still hunts in packs like the original stock
options.explanation: Pack hunting is not what the example demonstrates; the point is bred variation.

options.text: dogs were shaped by natural selection alone
options.explanation: The dog example is powerful precisely because humans directed the change.

options.text: all breeds carry exactly the same genes
options.explanation: Breed differences rest on differing allele combinations, not identical genes.

check.stem: How long must the selection loop run before a new animal breed is declared?

options.text: Across many generations of offspring
options.explanation: Correct — repetition over generations is what makes the line reliable.

options.text: Through a single mating season
options.explanation: One season selects parents and produces young, but cannot establish a breed.
options.misconception: stops the loop after one round

options.text: Until the first litter is born
options.explanation: A first litter only begins the screening; the loop must continue.
options.misconception: confuses first offspring with a breed

options.text: For exactly one pair of parents
options.explanation: A breed is built from repeated selections, not one pairing.

check.stem: State which young are kept as breeding stock after each mating round.
check.modelAnswer: The young that express the desired characteristic are kept and mated on; animals without it leave the breeding line.

check.stem: List three livestock traits farmers commonly select for.
check.modelAnswer: High milk or meat output, larger hen eggs, and better wool quality are all common selection goals, alongside gentle temperament in dogs and speed in horses.

check.stem: Explain why the breeding loop must be repeated rather than stopped after one mating.
check.modelAnswer: One mating produces only some offspring that show the trait; repeating selection across many generations concentrates it until the whole breed reliably displays the feature.

check.stem: A farmer wants a flock that clips more wool each season. Describe the breeding programme.
check.modelAnswer: Choose the sheep with the heaviest fleece as parents, mate them, keep the heaviest-clipped lambs as the next stock, and repeat for many generations until high wool yield is standard.

lessons.title: Natural versus Artificial Selection
sourceHeadings: Natural selection vs artificial selection table
lessons.opening: The same word — selection — covers two very different processes. In nature, individuals with features suited to their environment survive and reproduce, and the change usually unfolds slowly. Under human direction, only animals carrying features people find useful are allowed to breed, so the population shifts within far fewer generations — although the features favoured need not help the animal's own survival.
keyPoints: Natural selection happens without human involvement; artificial selection happens only when humans choose the breeders.
Natural selection spreads features that improve survival and environmental fit; artificial selection spreads features valued by people, which can be useless or even harmful to the individual animal.
Natural selection usually works over long stretches of time; artificial selection moves faster because only feature-carrying animals reproduce.
A high-scoring exam answer always notes the repeated generations in artificial selection — a single pairing is not enough to create a breed.

low.restatement: Nature selects for survival and takes ages; people select for usefulness and get results quickly.
low.analogy: One is a wind dispersing seeds wherever they land; the other is a gardener planting only the seeds chosen on purpose.
low.examPointer: Three contrast rows win the marks: who intervenes, what the outcome favours, and how fast the change arrives.

medium.restatement: Natural selection filters variants by survival and reproduction in the wild over long periods, whereas artificial selection restricts reproduction to animals with human-valued features, driving change in fewer generations regardless of survival value.
medium.analogy: Natural selection is an open audition cast by the environment; artificial selection is a director who hires only performers that fit the script, whatever the talent market says.
medium.examPointer: Pair 'useful to humans' against 'not necessarily useful to the individual' — that asymmetry is the discriminator examiners look for.

check.stem: Which statement separates artificial from natural selection?

options.text: Humans decide which animals breed
options.explanation: Correct — human choice of breeders is the defining difference.

options.text: Only the fittest survive to reproduce
options.explanation: That describes natural selection; artificial selection lets chosen animals reproduce regardless of fitness.

options.text: It cannot change a population's appearance
options.explanation: Both processes shift population features; the agent differs, not the capacity to change.

options.text: It always improves survival in the wild
options.explanation: Human-valued features need not help wild survival at all.

check.stem: A feature bred for human benefit may reduce the individual's survival chances. Which process does this describe?

options.text: Artificial selection
options.explanation: Correct — human-valued features can trade against the animal's own survival.

options.text: Natural selection
options.explanation: Natural selection spreads survival-improving features, not human-preferred ones.

options.text: Genetic engineering
options.explanation: This comparison concerns selection processes, not laboratory gene transfer.

options.text: Asexual reproduction
options.explanation: Animal breeding is sexual; reproduction mode is not the discriminator here.

check.stem: Why does artificial selection usually move faster than natural selection?

options.text: Only animals with the wanted feature are allowed to reproduce
options.explanation: Correct — restricting breeders accelerates the spread of the feature.

options.text: Mutations happen more often on farms
options.explanation: Mutation rates do not rise because of farming; the speed comes from controlled reproduction.

options.text: Animals mutate when domesticated
options.explanation: Domestication does not cause mutation; selection chooses among existing variation.

options.text: Natural selection has stopped operating
options.explanation: Natural selection continues; artificial selection simply overlays human choice.
options.misconception: claims one process excludes the other

check.stem: Which outcome belongs to natural selection rather than artificial selection?

options.text: A population better fitted to its environment
options.explanation: Correct — environmental fit is nature's criterion, not a breeder's.

options.text: A herd yielding more milk
options.explanation: Milk yield is a human-valued production trait, the work of breeders.

options.text: A dog line with a gentler temperament
options.explanation: Temperament for owners is human-directed, not environmental fit.

options.text: A flock producing heavier fleece
options.explanation: Fleece weight serves the wool trade — a human goal.

check.stem: What must an exam answer about creating a new breed always include?

options.text: Repeating the selection over many generations
options.explanation: Correct — generational repetition is the required element of the answer.

options.text: The Latin name of the species
options.explanation: Naming conventions earn no selection marks here.

options.text: A Punnett square of the first mating
options.explanation: Inheritance diagrams are not required to describe the breeding loop.

options.text: The number of chromosomes involved
options.explanation: Chromosome counts play no part in the breeding-loop answer.

check.stem: State the two forces compared when describing selection types.
check.modelAnswer: Natural selection, which acts without human input, and artificial selection, which depends on humans choosing the breeders.

check.stem: State what artificial selection produces that may not help survival.
check.modelAnswer: Features valued by people, such as appearance or yield, which are not necessarily useful — and can even be harmful — to the individual animal.

check.stem: Explain why a feature favoured by breeders might spread even though it harms survival.
check.modelAnswer: Because humans, not the environment, decide which animals breed, a trait people value is passed on regardless of its survival cost.

check.stem: A breeder claims one mating between two fast horses created a new breed. Assess the claim.
check.modelAnswer: The claim fails: a new breed requires selecting offspring with the desired feature and repeating the process over many generations, not a single pairing.

figures.caption: Selective breeding has produced many different breeds of domestic dog

glossary.definition: Choosing parents with wanted features and breeding them over generations so their offspring carry those features.
The human-directed form of selection in which people decide which animals mate.
A lineage produced by repeated selection that reliably shows the chosen features.
An observable feature of an animal that can be passed to offspring.
